content:
Availability: generally available to all partners.

Looking for the other direction? This guide is about using Thread’s tools *from* your own agent. To bring external tools (Linear, Notion, Zapier) *into* Super Magic, see **Add External Tools to Super Magic with Connectors**.

## Overview

Thread exposes its service-desk actions over the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io), so any MCP-capable client — Claude Desktop, ChatGPT, Claude Code, Cursor, partner agents, your own app — can drive Thread workflows the same way Super Magic does in-product: search tickets, look up clients and devices, and (with the right permissions) take real actions.

```
Endpoint:   <https://api.getthread.com/mcp>
Transport:  Streamable HTTP
Auth:       OAuth 2.1 — sign in with your Thread account (no tokens to manage)
```

`https://api.getthread.com/mcp/thread` is a supported alias for the same server — use it if a client’s connector directory already has a “thread” entry, or to keep the name unambiguous when you connect multiple MCP servers.

Once connected, you can ask your assistant to do real work in Thread:

> “Create a ticket for Acme Corp: user can’t print, high priority.”

> “Show my open tickets for Globex.”

> “Add a note to ticket 12345 and log 30 minutes.”

> “Look up the contact Jane Doe and her recent tickets.”

> “Search our knowledge base for the VPN setup article.”

The assistant acts **as you**: it can only see and do what you can in Thread, in your workspace.

## Before you start

- A **Thread account** with login access.

### Get your connector URL

1. In Thread Inbox, select **Magic** in the left navigation, then **Connectors**.
2. Scroll to the **Thread MCP access** section.
3. Click **Copy** next to the connector URL:

```
<https://api.getthread.com/mcp>
```

If the section says **Connecting AI apps is turned off for your account**, a workspace admin has limited who can connect AI apps. Ask an admin for access. See [Control who can connect AI apps to Thread MCP](/super-magic/control-who-can-connect-ai-apps-to-thread-mcp).

## Connect your client

- Claude Desktop
- ChatGPT
- Claude Code (CLI)
- Other clients (Cursor, …)

1

Add a custom connector

**Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector**

2

Paste the URL

Paste the connector URL and click **Add**, then **Connect / Log in**

3

Sign in with Thread

A browser window opens — **sign in with your Thread account** and approve

4

Finish

Done — Thread’s tools appear in Claude. No token needed.

### Add Thread for everyone on a Claude Team or Enterprise plan

Each connection signs in as one Thread member, so there’s no single switch that connects your whole organization. On a Claude Team or Enterprise plan, a Claude Owner can add Thread to the organization’s connector list once, and each person then connects with their own Thread account.

1

Add the connector to your Claude organization

A Claude Owner or Primary Owner goes to **Organization settings → Connectors** in Claude, clicks **Add**, chooses **Custom → Web**, names the connector (for example, “Thread”), and pastes the connector URL. Keep sign-in on so each person authenticates individually, and don’t add a shared API key or request header.

2

Each person connects

Each member goes to **Customize → Connectors** in Claude, finds Thread in the list, clicks **Connect**, and signs in with their own Thread account.

Each person’s tool list follows their own Thread role and permissions (see Permissions). Anthropic documents the Claude-side steps and the roles that can add organization connectors in [Get started with custom connectors using remote MCP](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11175166-getting-started-with-custom-connectors-using-remote-mcp).

## Microsoft Copilot: two different products, both supported

Microsoft ships two Copilot products that both let you connect an MCP server, and they look similar enough to mix up. Both work with Thread MCP, but they set up differently.

| Microsoft product | Supported with Thread MCP? | What it asks for at setup |
|---|---|---|
| **Copilot Studio** (the agent builder) | **Yes**: use this today | Just the Thread MCP URL. Sign in with a Thread account when prompted. |
| **Microsoft 365 Copilot custom federated connectors** | **Yes**: read-only | A **Reference ID** and OAuth **Client ID / Secret**. A Thread workspace admin creates the credentials in Thread’s Inbox. See Microsoft 365 Copilot federated connectors. |

### Connect Copilot Studio to Thread MCP

Copilot Studio is Microsoft’s low-code agent builder. Add Thread MCP as a tool on the agent that should use it:

1

Open the agent's Tools tab

In Copilot Studio, open the agent you want to give Thread access to, then open its **Tools** page.

2

Add a new MCP tool

Select **Add a tool → New tool → Model Context Protocol**. Copilot Studio’s MCP onboarding wizard opens.

3

Fill in the server details

- **Server name**: `Thread`. Copilot Studio turns this into a Power Platform custom connector, so the name has to be unused in the environment. Keep it to plain words: no periods, and no version numbers like `Thread 2.0`.
- **Server description**: a short line the orchestrator uses to decide when to call Thread, for example: *Thread service-desk actions: search and update tickets, look up clients and contacts, log time.*
- **Server URL**: `https://api.getthread.com/mcp`
- **Transport**: Streamable HTTP (Copilot Studio’s default)

4

Set Authentication to OAuth 2.0, Dynamic (with discovery)

Select **Authentication → OAuth 2.0**, then set **Configuration type** to **Dynamic (with discovery)**. That is the whole configuration: Thread’s MCP server publishes OAuth 2.1 discovery metadata and supports dynamic client registration, so Copilot Studio finds the endpoints and registers itself at creation time.Leave every credential field empty, and do not choose **Manual**. Manual asks for a Reference ID, Client ID, and Client Secret. The only credentials Thread issues are for Microsoft 365 Copilot federated connectors, and they only accept the Teams Developer Portal redirect URI, so they don’t work in Copilot Studio. Microsoft describes all three configuration types in [Configure OAuth 2.0 authentication](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-copilot-studio/mcp-add-existing-server-to-agent#configure-oauth-20-authentication).

5

Create the connection and sign in with Thread

Select **Create**, then **Next**. On **Add tool**, select **Create a new connection**. A browser window opens: sign in with your Thread account, approve, then select **Add to agent**.

6

Add the tools you want to expose

Back on the tool’s settings page, Copilot Studio lists every Thread tool your account can see. Leave **Allow all** on to expose everything, or turn it off to pick individual tools (for example, only reads). Save.

The agent can now call Thread. Ask it something like *“Show my open tickets for Acme”* to confirm end-to-end.

#### ”Can’t create MCP server. Try again.”

This error fires before Copilot Studio ever contacts Thread. It means Copilot Studio could not create the Power Platform custom connector it builds behind the scenes, so nothing on Thread’s side will fix it. Work through these in order:

1

Delete the orphaned connector from your last attempt

This is the usual cause, and Microsoft confirms it in [this Q&A thread](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/5862279/adding-mcp-server-as-tool-in-copilot-studio-fails): when MCP onboarding fails partway, the custom connector is still written to Dataverse but never appears in the Copilot Studio UI, and every later attempt collides with it, **including attempts under a new name**. Open [make.powerapps.com](https://make.powerapps.com), confirm you are in the same environment, then go to **Custom connectors** and delete anything Thread-shaped. Wait two or three minutes for metadata to sync before retrying.

2

Simplify the server name

Retry as `Thread`. A name carrying a period or a version suffix becomes a connector logical name and is a needless risk.

3

Check your environment permissions

Creating a custom connector needs system administrator rights on the target Power Platform environment. Ask your Power Platform admin to confirm yours, or switch to an environment you own.

4

Move off the default environment

Tenant-level data loss prevention policies commonly block custom connectors in the **default** environment, and MCP tools inherit them because Copilot Studio reaches an MCP server through a Power Platform connector. Try a dedicated development environment instead, and see Microsoft’s [MCP servers and data policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-copilot-studio/mcp-add-existing-server-to-agent#mcp-servers-and-data-policies) and [Configure a data policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-copilot-studio/admin-data-loss-prevention#configure-a-data-policy-in-the-power-platform-admin-center).

5

Click outside the URL field, then Create again

The wizard sometimes leaves **Server URL** showing “Enter the complete server path to continue” and the **Create** button looking disabled when the URL is in fact valid. Click anywhere outside the field, then select **Create**.

If the server still will not create, switch **Configuration type** from **Dynamic (with discovery)** to **Dynamic** and supply the two endpoints by hand. It is the same registration flow with discovery skipped:

- **Authorization URL**: `https://api.getthread.com/oauth/authorize`
- **Token URL template**: `https://api.getthread.com/oauth/token`

Still avoid **Manual** as a workaround. It requires a client ID and secret preissued by the MCP server. Thread’s connector credentials are bound to the Microsoft 365 Copilot redirect URI, so they don’t work in Copilot Studio. If a field insists on them, you are likely on the Microsoft 365 Copilot federated connectors path below.

Microsoft’s own references for this section:

- [Connect your agent to an existing MCP server](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-copilot-studio/mcp-add-existing-server-to-agent), the onboarding wizard end to end, including [supported transports](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-copilot-studio/mcp-add-existing-server-to-agent#supported-transports) and [Configure OAuth 2.0 authentication](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-copilot-studio/mcp-add-existing-server-to-agent#configure-oauth-20-authentication).
- [Add MCP tools and resources to your agent](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-copilot-studio/mcp-add-components-to-agent), for picking which Thread tools the agent may call.
- [Adding MCP servers as a tool fails](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/5862279/adding-mcp-server-as-tool-in-copilot-studio-fails), Microsoft’s Q&A thread on orphaned custom connectors.
- [Configure a data policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-copilot-studio/admin-data-loss-prevention#configure-a-data-policy-in-the-power-platform-admin-center), if your environment blocks custom connectors.

### Microsoft 365 Copilot federated connectors

Microsoft 365 Copilot custom federated connectors is a different product. It makes an external data source searchable inside Microsoft 365 Copilot. Its setup dialog for an MCP endpoint asks for:

- A **Reference ID**: an id from a Microsoft-side OAuth registration in the Teams Developer Portal.
- An OAuth **Client ID and Client Secret**: credentials the MCP server issues to the connector.

Thread issues the client ID and secret per workspace. Use this path when you want Thread data available inside Microsoft 365 Copilot itself rather than in a Copilot Studio agent.

Federated connector credentials are read-only. Tokens issued through them carry only the `mcp:read` scope, so Thread’s write tools (creating or updating tickets, logging time) are never available through a federated connector. Use Copilot Studio if your agent needs write tools.

**Prerequisites:**

- Thread MCP enabled for your workspace (see Before you start).
- A Thread workspace admin or team admin role. Other roles don’t see the Microsoft 365 Copilot section.
- Access to the [Teams Developer Portal](https://dev.teams.microsoft.com) and the Microsoft 365 admin center for your tenant.

1

Create connector credentials in Thread

In Thread’s Inbox, open **Settings → Connectors** and scroll to **Microsoft 365 Copilot**. Select **New connector**, enter a name (for example, `M365 Copilot`), and select **Create**.

2

Copy the credentials

The **Connector credentials** dialog shows the client secret once. Copy it before you close the dialog with **I’ve saved my secret**. Thread stores only a hash and can’t show the secret again.The dialog also lists the values to register with Microsoft:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Client ID | Shown in the dialog |
| Client secret | Shown once in the dialog |
| Authorization endpoint | Shown in the dialog |
| Token endpoint | Shown in the dialog |
| Refresh endpoint | Shown in the dialog |
| Scopes | `mcp:read` |
| Redirect URI | `https://teams.microsoft.com/api/platform/v1.0/oAuthRedirect` |
| MCP endpoint URL | Shown in the dialog |

3

Register the client in the Teams Developer Portal

In the Teams Developer Portal, open **Tools → OAuth Client Registration** and register a client with the values from the dialog. Microsoft returns a registration ID.

4

Finish the connector in the Microsoft 365 admin center

In the federated connector setup, enter the MCP endpoint URL and paste the Teams registration ID as the **Reference ID**.

Thread binds each credential to your workspace. When a user signs in through the connector, Thread’s consent screen only offers that workspace. To manage existing credentials, use the list under **Microsoft 365 Copilot** in **Settings → Connectors**:

- **Rotate secret** issues a new secret and invalidates the old one immediately. The connector stops working until you paste the new secret into the Teams Developer Portal registration.
- **Revoke** disables the credential permanently. Its status changes to **Revoked**.

## Automation keys: connect without a browser

OAuth sign-in needs a browser. Some clients never get one: n8n, CI pipelines, and other server-side automations. For those, Thread supports **automation keys**: personal access tokens that authenticate against the same MCP endpoint with a static bearer credential instead of a sign-in. Who can mint one:

- Any member can mint a key bound to themselves.
- **Workspace admins** can mint a key for any active member in the workspace.
- **Team admins** can mint a key for members on their own teams, but not for workspace admins.

Workspace admins and team admins can mint and revoke keys from Thread Admin: open **Admin → Thread MCP → MCP keys**, select **Generate token**, then pick the member, name the key, and set an expiry. The page also lists the keys you can manage with each key’s bound member and issuer: every key in the workspace for workspace admins, or keys for members on their teams for team admins. Alternatively, mint a key with a `POST` to `/api/v1/mcp/tokens` on Thread’s API, authenticated as the issuing member:

```
{
  "name": "n8n ticket sync",
  "expires_at": "2027-03-01T00:00:00Z",
  "member_id": 4821
}
```

- `name`, a label so you can tell keys apart later (required).
- `expires_at` — when the key stops working. Optional for a key bound to yourself, required when minting for another member, and never more than one year out.
- `member_id`, the member the key acts as. Omit it to bind the key to yourself. Sending it without admin rights returns `403`.

The response includes the key’s plaintext value (it starts with `mcp_`) **exactly once**. Store it in your secret manager — Thread keeps only a hash and cannot show it again. Use the key as a bearer token wherever your MCP client accepts auth headers:

```
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "thread": {
      "url": "https://api.getthread.com/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer mcp_…" }
    }
  }
}
```

A key behaves exactly like a signed-in connection for its member: same tool list, same permissions, same audit trail. Keys also follow the workspace’s **Who can connect apps** setting: a member who isn’t allowed to connect can’t be issued a key, and their existing keys are revoked when an admin restricts access. Each key also records which member issued it, so admins can see who minted a key for whom.

Notes written through a key appear in your PSA under the bound member, so bind keys to a dedicated automation member linked to a PSA user rather than a real technician. Status and other ticket field changes appear as your PSA API user. The full walkthrough is in [Issue MCP automation keys for team members](/super-magic/issue-mcp-automation-keys-for-team-members).

To revoke a key, send `DELETE /api/v1/mcp/tokens/{id}` — connections using it stop working immediately. List keys beyond your own with `GET /api/v1/mcp/tokens?scope=company`: workspace admins see every key in the workspace, and team admins see keys for members on their teams, plus their own. Revoking follows the same scope; a key outside it returns a not-found error.

## Permissions: every connection sees a different tool list

The server registers tools **per connection**, applying exactly the permissions that member has in Super Magic:

| Gate | Effect on the tool list |
|---|---|
| Who can connect apps | If an admin set **Admin → Thread MCP → Connected apps → Who can connect apps** to a level the member doesn’t pass, Thread refuses the connection and the client gets an access error |
| Member role | Intent and flow tools appear only for workspace admins |
| Workspace plan | On a non-Agentic plan (no AI Pro), the connection sees only the seven read-only Super Magic tools, the same surface Super Magic exposes in the inbox. Write and integration tools appear only on Agentic plans. |
| Workspace write access level | Write tools (create/update ticket, notes, time, approvals…) appear only if the member passes it (All members / Admins only / Custom list) |
| Per-tool toggles | A write tool an admin switched off disappears for everyone |
| Integrations | NinjaOne / ImmyBot / TimeZest / IT Glue / Hudu tools appear only when the integration is configured + enabled. NinjaOne additionally requires the member’s own sign-in |

### Not every Super Magic tool is exposed over MCP

Thread MCP exposes a **curated subset** of Super Magic’s tools. Every tool on the MCP server is a Super Magic tool with the same name and the same gating, but the reverse doesn’t hold. Some Super Magic tools never appear over MCP, no matter how the workspace is configured:

- **Liongard**: Super Magic-only, in both forms (the workspace integration and the per-member connector). Connecting Liongard and turning on its Super Magic toggle adds Liongard tools in Inbox chat, but an MCP client will never list them.
- **Per-member connector tools** (Linear, Notion, Zapier) — these register inside Super Magic only.

To use those tools, run the request in Super Magic in Inbox (or a Companion App) instead of your external client. The [tool reference](/super-magic/super-magic-tool-reference) is the canonical list of what each surface exposes. Practical consequence: **don’t hardcode the tool list.** Call `tools/list` and work with what’s there. A read-only member’s connection registers only read tools; an admin on a fully-integrated workspace can see 50+. The connection only ever touches **your workspace’s** data.

## Typical workflows

**Discover ids, then write.** Ticket writes take internal ids — resolve them first:

1. `search_clients` → `client_company_id`
2. `list_boards`, `list_ticket_statuses`, `list_ticket_priorities` → board/status/priority ids
3. `create_ticket` / `update_ticket` / `add_ticket_note` / `log_time_entry` with those ids

**Look up before acting.** `search_tickets` accepts a PSA ticket number or internal id and returns `internal_ticket_id` — pass *that* to write tools. **Classify tickets (ConnectWise and HaloPSA):** on ConnectWise workspaces, `list_board_classifications` returns the Type → Subtype → Item tree for a ticket’s board; pass the resolved ids to `set_ticket_classification`. Passing only `item_id` sets all three levels without disturbing the existing Type or Subtype — see the [tool reference](/super-magic/super-magic-tool-reference) for the full id cascade. On HaloPSA workspaces the same pair works on Category 1: `list_board_classifications` returns a flat list of Category 1 values, and `set_ticket_classification` takes `type_id` alone (`subtype_id` and `item_id` are rejected). **Device workflows (NinjaOne connected):** `search_ninjaone_devices` → `get_ninjaone_device` / `list_ninjaone_alerts` → `reboot_ninjaone_device` etc. To scope by device type (“all Linux servers”, “every Windows workstation”) pass the `device_class` parameter instead of putting the OS name in `query`. `query` only matches hostname and last-logged-in user, so `query: "linux"` returns whatever happens to have “linux” in its name, not Linux machines. **Admin automation:** intent and flow tools let an admin connection inspect and build workspace automations programmatically.

## Rate limits

The Thread MCP endpoints (`/mcp` and `/mcp/thread`) enforce two layers of throttling. Both apply per minute and use a rolling one-minute window:

| Layer | Bucket | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-auth IP backstop | Client IP | 1,200 requests / minute |
| Per-company tenant limit | Workspace (company) | 300 requests / minute |

PAT and OAuth clients for the same workspace share a single per-company bucket, so mixing auth methods does not raise your effective limit. The Thread MCP bucket is separate from those of Thread’s other integrations, so hitting one server’s limit never affects the other. When you exceed a limit, the server responds with `HTTP 429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header (in seconds). Wait for that duration before retrying — clients should implement exponential backoff on 429s and honor `Retry-After`. If you regularly bump into these limits, batch requests where possible, cache lookups like `list_boards` / `list_ticket_statuses` / `list_ninjaone_organizations` locally, and contact your Thread account team about a higher tenant limit.

## Security model

- **You authorize by signing in**: no secrets to paste, store, or rotate for the one-click path.
- **Least privilege by construction**: a connection can never do more than its member can in the product. To restrict an external agent, restrict the member.
- **Admins control who can connect**: workspace admins choose All members, Only admins, Custom or Off for everyone, see every connected app, and revoke any of them from **Admin → Thread MCP → Connected apps**. See [Control who can connect AI apps to Thread MCP](/super-magic/control-who-can-connect-ai-apps-to-thread-mcp).
- **Disconnect**: members can disconnect their own apps from Inbox under **Magic → Connectors → Your connected apps**. To be sure an app is cut off, disconnect or revoke it in Thread rather than only removing it in the AI client.
- **Audit**: every tool call is logged under the member identity behind the connection.

## Errors & troubleshooting

| Symptom | Meaning | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| ”Your account has no active Thread membership” | Signed into an account that isn’t an active member of a Thread workspace | Sign in with the right account |
| Tools don’t appear / connection fails | URL typo, sign-in not completed, or stale client state | Re-check the exact URL, finish the sign-in, then quit and relaunch the client |
| ”Couldn’t load the connector URL. Please refresh.” on the Connectors page | Thread Inbox couldn’t fetch the connector URL | Refresh the page; if it persists, contact Thread support |
| Login opens but errors out | Transient auth issue | Retry from a fresh browser session; if it persists, contact Thread support |
| All Thread tools disappear, or Inbox says “Connecting AI apps is turned off for your account” | A workspace admin restricted who can connect apps, or revoked this app | Ask an admin to check **Admin → Thread MCP → Connected apps**. Once you’re allowed again, connect the app again |
| A tool you expect isn’t in tools/list | Per-connection visibility (matrix above) | Check the member’s role, write access, the tool’s toggle, and integration state |
| A tool works in Super Magic in Inbox but never appears over MCP | The tool is Super Magic-only: Liongard and per-member connector tools (Linear, Notion, Zapier) are not exposed over Thread MCP | Run that request in Super Magic in Inbox or a Companion App instead |
| Copilot Studio: “Can’t create MCP server. Try again.” | Copilot Studio could not create its own Power Platform custom connector, usually colliding with an orphaned one from a failed attempt | Work through “Can’t create MCP server. Try again.” above |
| Copilot Studio asks for a Client ID and Secret | **Configuration type** is set to **Manual**, or you are in Microsoft 365 Copilot federated connectors rather than Copilot Studio | Set **Configuration type** to **Dynamic (with discovery)**; if the fields persist, you are on the federated connector path. Follow Microsoft 365 Copilot federated connectors |

## Tool reference

Full tool-by-tool documentation: [**Super Magic Tool Reference**](/super-magic/super-magic-tool-reference).
